newsitem.title: UK: Copper pulls LME lower, markets end soft.
newsitem.headline: Copper pulls LME lower, markets end soft.

text.p: Copper prices took a beating during Friday afternoon LME ring and kerb trading, with the market ending at its lows and set to re-visit the levels below $1,900, traders said.
Copper's downturn followed another failure overhead around the $1,950 level, a deteriorating chart picture, widespread speculative sales and the establishment of a broader contango structure nearby.
After briefly touching a contango in mid-week for the first time since January 1995, there is now a hint of permanance in the current cash metal discounts.
"It just goes to show you that the market has been basically manipulated for years," one copper trader said.

Cash/threes, which was at a $19 backwardation a week ago, finished at $11/13 contango today, against Thursday's small $4 cash discount. Further forward the backwardations at the end of this year and the beginning of 1997 are also waning.

Traders said lenders are looking to take advantage of these disappearing premiums, as the market's fundamental picture post-Sumitomo becomes clearer. Despite falling LME warehouse stocks and a pick-up in physical interest in Europe the market now believes that oversupply will be the feature in 1997.
Three months ended the kerb at $1,900 a tonne, down $36 from Thursday's kerb close. The next objective is $1,870, traders said.

Aluminium managed to claw its way up from a fresh 2-1/4 year low of $1,403, as end-week covering and technical support between $1,400 and $1,410 came into play. But prices finished at $1,412, still down $16.

Traders said the market is likely to fall below $1,400 soon, with fundamentals all depressive. LME warehouse stocks are seen continuing to rise, following Friday's 4,825-tonne increase. Also, August IPAI production data showed output is inching up.

Nickel gradually lost ground during a sluggish session, although price movements were largely low-key and late covering kept losses to a minimum. The 594-tonne stock increase, although expected, also put some pressure on the market.

In the short-term the market will continue to adopt a cautious policy over the ongoing Inco dispute in Canada, although there has been no impcat on supplies so far. Last trade was at $7,380 a tonne, a $10 loss from Thursday's kerb close.
Zinc prices crumbled during the late afternoon, although declines were cushioned just under $1,030, and the market is likely to remain comfortable between $1,030/40.
The 850-tonne stock drawdown was not particularly large, but maintained the recent trend. Zinc ended the kerb at $1,030, down $5.50.
Lead also fell away during the afternoon session, reflecting another stock increase, the overall LME trend, and lacklustre conditions. Last business was at $782, down $5 from Thursday.
Tin trading was restricted to a narrow range, with some trade buying and technical support holding the market above $6,100. The market finished at $6,100/05, against the previous close of $6,119.
Alloy was marked lower with primary, and ended at $1,232/40 a tonne, down from the overnight $1,240/45.
